name: Battle of the Somme
info: British Empire and French armies attacked the German Second Army on both sides of the upper Somme from 1 July to 18 November 1916, gaining about 10 km at a cost of over a million casualties.

facts.place: Both sides of the upper reaches of the river Somme in Picardy, northern France
facts.sides: The British Fourth Army under Sir Henry Rawlinson, with the Third Army and later the Reserve Army under Hubert Gough, and the French Sixth Army under Émile Fayolle, under the overall direction of Douglas Haig and Joseph Joffre, against the German Second Army under Fritz von Below; more than three million men fought in all
facts.outcome: The Allies advanced about 10 km along most of the front, their largest gain since the Marne in 1914, but did not take Péronne or Bapaume; casualties on all sides exceeded one million, and the German army withdrew to the Hindenburg Line in March 1917.

t: The first day, 1 July 1916, cost the British 57,470 casualties, 19,240 of them killed, the worst in the history of the British Army, most of them north of the Albert–Bapaume road; the French Sixth Army lost 1,590.

The plan changed as the war went on: Verdun drew off French divisions, so the offensive in which the French were to take the main part became a mainly British effort, and a hoped-for decisive victory was reduced to relieving Verdun and wearing down the German army.
Casualty counts are disputed: British 419,654 to 432,000, French about 200,000, and German anywhere from 400,000 to 680,000 depending on the historian and the method of counting.
dyk: Before the attack on 1 July the British artillery fired more than 1.5 million shells in the preliminary bombardment, more than in the first year of the war, and the guns could be heard on Hampstead Heath, 165 miles (266 km) away.
ev: The Chantilly Conference agrees simultaneous Allied offensives for 1916 and the Franco-British contribution is planned for the Somme
The German attack on Verdun begins on 21 February and French divisions meant for the Somme are diverted there
On 1 July the British Fourth Army and the French Sixth Army attack the German Second Army after a bombardment that began on 24 June
On 14 July the Fourth Army attacks the German second position at Bazentin Ridge after a five-minute hurricane bombardment
On 15 September tanks, the Canadian Corps and the New Zealand Division make their debut on the Somme at Flers–Courcelette
The last big British operation of the year, the Battle of the Ancre, is fought from 13 to 18 November
British attacks on the Ancre from January force local German withdrawals, followed by Operation Alberich and the retirement to the Hindenburg Line from 16 March

sections.background:
Allied strategy for 1916 was decided at the Chantilly Conference from 6 to 8 December 1915. Offensives by the Russian army on the Eastern Front, the Italian army on the Italian Front and the Franco-British armies on the Western Front were to be carried out at the same time, so that the Central Powers had no time to move troops between fronts. That month General Sir Douglas Haig replaced Field Marshal Sir John French as Commander-in-Chief of the British Expeditionary Force (BEF) and favoured an offensive in Flanders. In February 1916 it was decided to attack first where the French and British armies met, astride the Somme in Picardy.

A week later the Germans began the Battle of Verdun, on 21 February. The costly defence of Verdun forced the French to divert divisions intended for the Somme and eventually reduced their contribution to 13 divisions in the Sixth Army, against 20 British divisions. The British attack, first meant as support, became the principal effort. By 31 May the plan for a decisive victory had shrunk to a limited offensive to relieve pressure on the French at Verdun and inflict attrition on the German armies in the west, and on 16 June Haig defined the objectives in those terms.

The Chief of the German General Staff, Erich von Falkenhayn, meant to end the war by splitting the Entente. He expected the French to suffer huge losses at Verdun and the British relief offensive to fall south of Arras and be destroyed. The Brusilov offensive, which began on 4 June, absorbed forces that the German Second Army had asked for to make a spoiling attack on the Somme.
sections.forces:
The British Fourth Army under General Sir Henry Rawlinson was to take 27,000 yards (25,000 m) of the German first line from Montauban to Serre after a five-day bombardment, with the Third Army making a diversion at Gommecourt. The BEF was made up largely of wartime volunteers of the Territorial Force and Kitchener's Army, with the remains of the pre-war army, and rapid expansion had lowered its average experience. The French Sixth Army had one corps on the north bank and two on the south, and made a subsidiary attack to guard the British right flank. The attack was made by five French divisions east of the Somme, eleven British divisions of the Fourth Army and two of the Third Army, against the German Second Army under General Fritz von Below.

German defences on the Somme had been built up since January 1915. Barbed wire was laid in two belts about 30 yards deep, the front position had three trench lines 150 to 200 yards apart, dugouts had been deepened to 20 to 30 feet, and a line of strongpoints stood about 1,000 yards behind. A second position lay beyond the range of Allied field artillery. The front trenches were on a forward slope, lined with white chalk and easy to see, and the garrisons were crowded close to them. Research in German archives revealed in 2016 that two disgruntled soldiers had betrayed the date and place of the British offensive weeks before. Falkenhayn sent only four divisions to the Somme although an attack was certain by mid-June.
sections.course:
The Allied bombardment began on 24 June, and the infantry attacked on 1 July on both banks of the Somme. The French Sixth Army and the right wing of the Fourth Army inflicted a considerable defeat on the German Second Army, but from the Albert–Bapaume road to Gommecourt the attack was a disaster, where most of the British casualties occurred. Haig, against Joffre's wishes, abandoned the offensive north of the road to reinforce success in the south. Fighting then became a series of attacks on fortified villages and woods. The Fourth Army attacked at Bazentin Ridge on 14 July at 3:25 a.m., after a five-minute hurricane bombardment. The 1st Australian Division captured Pozières on 23 July, and Delville Wood was held by the South African brigade from 15 to 20 July.

Guillemont was captured on 3 to 6 September and Ginchy on 9 September. On 15 September the Battle of Flers–Courcelette began: it was the third and final general offensive by the British Army, and the first appearance on the Somme of the Canadian Corps, the New Zealand Division and tanks. It advanced the front by 2,500 to 3,500 yards but did not achieve a breakthrough. Morval and Thiepval Ridge followed on 25 to 28 September. In October and November, with rain and mud, the Battles of Le Transloy and the Ancre Heights ran from 1 October to 11 November, and the Battle of the Ancre, from 13 to 18 November, was the last big British operation of the year.
sections.aftermath:
At the end of the battle British and French forces had penetrated 6.2 miles (10 km) into German-occupied territory along most of the front, their largest gain since the First Battle of the Marne in 1914. They had not captured Péronne or Bapaume, where the German armies held their positions over the winter. British casualties are put at 419,654 to 432,000, French at about 200,000 and German at 465,181 to 500,000 or perhaps 600,000. Falkenhayn was replaced by Hindenburg and Ludendorff at the end of August 1916, and on 5 September a conference at Cambrai decided to build a new defensive line well behind the Somme front.

British attacks in the Ancre valley resumed in January 1917 and forced local German withdrawals in February, eventually taking 5,284 prisoners. The Germans then carried out a strategic retreat of about 25 miles (40 km) to the Siegfriedstellung, or Hindenburg Line, in Operation Alberich, which began on 16 March 1917 although the new line was unfinished. The Somme defences held by the Germans after November 1916 were in poor condition and the garrisons were exhausted. For Britain and its dominions the battle left a long memory, and some historians hold that it took the strategic initiative from the German army and began a process of attrition that led to its collapse in 1918.
sections.sources:
The battle is documented in the official histories of the belligerents and in many later studies, and the figures are still argued. The Allied estimate made at the Chantilly Conference on 15 November 1916 gave German casualties as 630,000, against 485,000 for the British and French. Modern scholars hold that this was exaggerated: German Reichsarchiv tabulations give 237,159 casualties of all types for the 69 divisions involved. J. E. Edmonds, the British official historian, gave in 1932 British casualties of 419,654, French of 194,451 and German of about 445,322 with 27 per cent added; Wilfrid Miles in 1938 gave German losses of 660,000 to 680,000. M. J. Williams called Edmonds's addition spurious in 1964, and Gary Sheffield in 2003 called it discredited and quoted 500,000 as the official German figure. William Philpott gave the German total as disputed, 400,000 to 680,000.

French figures include 202,567 (Doughty) and 154,446 for the Sixth Army with 48,131 for the Tenth (Philpott's sources). German and French writing on the battle has largely not been translated, which leaves much of its detail out of English-language histories. Research in German archives revealed in 2016 that the British plan had been betrayed to German interrogators.
sections.legacy:
In the United Kingdom and Newfoundland the Battle of the Somme became the central memory of the First World War. The Royal British Legion, the British Embassy in Paris and the Commonwealth War Graves Commission commemorate it each 1 July at the Thiepval Memorial to the Missing of the Somme. The 1st Newfoundland Regiment was named the Royal Newfoundland Regiment by George V on 28 November 1917, and the island remembers the day on the Sunday nearest 1 July. Northern Ireland remembers the battle through the 36th (Ulster) Division. On 1 July 2016 the United Kingdom held a two-minute silence at 7:28 a.m., and 1,400 actors in replica uniforms played the part of soldiers who had died on the first day.

Until the 1930s the dominant English-language view was that the battle was a hard-fought victory against a brave, experienced opponent. In the 1930s a new orthodoxy of mud, blood and futility emerged, and gained emphasis in the 1960s. Churchill objected to the way it was fought in August 1916, and Lloyd George condemned attrition warfare in his memoirs. John Terraine, Gary Sheffield, William Philpott and others hold that there was no strategic alternative for the British in 1916. In 2016 Peter Barton argued that the battle should be regarded as a German defensive victory.

summary: From 1 July to 18 November 1916 British and French armies attacked the German Second Army on both banks of the Somme. They gained about 10 km but did not take Péronne or Bapaume, and casualty counts are still disputed.
references: R. A. Doughty, Pyrrhic Victory: French Strategy and Operation in the Great War (The Belknap Press of Harvard University, 2005)
C. Duffy, Through German Eyes: The British and the Somme 1916 (Weidenfeld & Nicolson, 2006)
W. Philpott, Bloody Victory: The Sacrifice on the Somme and the Making of the Twentieth Century (Little, Brown, 2009)
J. Sheldon, The German Army on the Somme 1914–1916 (Leo Cooper, 2006)
